title: Cranberry Orange Loaf
steps:
Mix and Knead the Dough

This is a lightly enriched dough, soft from milk and butter, with orange juice doing double duty as liquid and flavor. The juice's acidity slows the yeast a touch, which is fine. It buys you flavor.

Zest first, then juice

Zest both oranges before you juice them. Rub the zest into the honey with your fingers for a minute. It sounds fussy, it isn't. The oils bloom into the honey and carry through the whole loaf.

Mix to a shaggy dough

Whisk the flour and instant yeast in the mixer bowl. Add the lukewarm milk, orange juice, and the honey-zest mixture. Mix on low until no dry flour remains, about 2 minutes, then rest 10 minutes so the flour hydrates.

Add salt and butter, then knead

Add the salt, then knead on medium while adding the soft butter a piece at a time. Keep going 8-10 minutes until the dough is smooth and passes the windowpane test. It should feel supple and slightly tacky, not sticky.

Fold in the cranberries

Pat the halved cranberries dry and toss them with the tablespoon of flour. Add them to the bowl and mix on the lowest speed 30-60 seconds, just until distributed. Overmix and they smear pink streaks through the dough. A few streaks are charming. A tie-dye loaf is not.

Bulk Ferment

One straight rise until doubled. This is also your Friday-night pause point if you'd rather bake with your coffee on Saturday.

Rise until doubled

Round the dough into an oiled bowl, cover, and let it rise 1 3/4 to 2 hours at 75°F (24°C), until doubled. The orange juice slows things slightly, so trust the size of the dough, not the clock.

Or pause here overnight

For the make-ahead route, put the covered bowl straight into the fridge after mixing and let the cold retard run 8-16 hours. Saturday morning, the dough is risen, cold, and easier to shape than it ever is warm. Shape it straight from the fridge and add 20-30 minutes to the final proof.

Shape the Loaf

A standard sandwich-loaf shape, done gently so the berries stay put.

Degas and pat out

Turn the dough onto a lightly floured counter and pat it into a rough 8x10 inch rectangle, pressing out the big bubbles. Any berries that pop out, tuck them back in. Berries on the surface scorch in the oven.

Roll and seal

With a short side facing you, roll the dough into a snug log, pressing the seam as you go. Pinch the final seam and the ends closed, then place it seam-side down in the greased 9x5 pan.

Shaping the Loaf — choose your method

Keep the tension even and the berries buried, and the loaf takes care of itself.

Standard Pan Loaf

The classic 9x5 sandwich shape.

Gently press the dough into an 8x10 inch rectangle, tucking any exposed berries back inside.
Roll from a short side into a tight log, pinch the seam and ends, and set it seam-down in the pan.

Proof, Bake, and Glaze

Moderate heat, a foil tent when it's bronzed, and a thermometer to call it done. The glaze goes on only after the loaf is fully cool.

OVEN
350°F (175°C)
DONE AT
190°F (88°C)

9x5 Loaf Pan (Recommended)

The standard method for both the yeasted and sourdough versions.

Equipment: 9x5 inch loaf pan

Final proof: Cover the pan loosely and proof 60-75 minutes, until the dough crowns about 1 inch above the rim. Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C) when the dough reaches the rim. If the dough was cold-retarded, expect 90-105 minutes.
Bake: Bake 40-45 minutes, until deep golden and 190°F (88°C) at the center. The honey and juice brown fast, so tent with foil around the 25-minute mark. Sourdough version runs about 5 minutes longer.

Cool completely: Cool in the pan 10 minutes, then turn out onto a rack. Let it cool at least 90 minutes before glazing or slicing. Warm bread plus glaze equals a puddle, and warm cranberry bread slices gummy.

Glaze (optional): Whisk the powdered sugar, orange juice, and zest until smooth. It should ribbon off the whisk and hold for a second. Drizzle over the cool loaf and let it set 20 minutes before slicing.

190°F (88°C) internal, no exceptions. The berries add moisture that fools the thump test.

RECIPE PANTRY
CRUST & CRUMB ACADEMY
FROM THE PANTRY OF HENRY HUNTER
Cranberry Orange Loaf

Soft Yeasted Loaf, Bright with Citrus

Soft yeasted cranberry orange loaf with fresh berries, zest, and juice in the dough. Includes a full sourdough version and an optional orange glaze.

YIELD
One 9x5 inch loaf, about 12 thick slices
PREP
30 minutes
BAKE
40-45 minutes at 350°F (175°C)
TOTAL
About 5 hours same-day, or split over two days with the cold retard
DOUGH (YEASTED VERSION)
500g
Bread flour
4 cups
160g
Whole milk, lukewarm (about 95°F / 35°C)
2/3 cup
130g
Fresh orange juice, room temperature
1/2 cup + 1 tbsp
40g
Honey
2 tbsp
50g
Unsalted butter, softened
3 1/2 tbsp
10g
Fine sea salt
1 3/4 tsp
7g
Instant yeast
2 1/4 tsp
12g
Orange zest (from 2 oranges)
2 tbsp
CRANBERRIES
150g
Fresh cranberries, halved (or frozen, unthawed)
1 1/2 cups
8g
Bread flour, for tossing the berries
1 tbsp
ORANGE GLAZE (OPTIONAL)
120g
Powdered sugar, sifted
1 cup
30ml
Fresh orange juice
2 tbsp
1g
Orange zest
1/2 tsp
BAKER'S PERCENTAGES
500g (100%)
Total flour
58%
Hydration
2%
Salt
EQUIPMENT
9x5 inch loaf pan
Stand mixer with dough hook (or a bowl and 15 minutes of hand kneading)
Digital scale
Microplane zester
Instant-read thermometer
Dough whisk (for the hand-mix crowd)
Cooling rack
Small whisk (for the glaze)
STORAGE
Room Temperature
3-4 days wrapped or in a bread bag. Glazed loaves keep best under a cake dome. Toast slices to refresh.
Frozen
Up to 3 months. Freeze unglazed if you can, sliced for easy toasting, and glaze after thawing.
Tip
Day-three slices make outrageous French toast.
QUESTIONS
Can I use dried cranberries instead of fresh?

Yes. Use 120g dried, soaked 20 minutes in hot orange juice, drained and patted dry. The loaf comes out sweeter and less tart than the fresh-berry version, so consider skipping the glaze.

Why did my dough turn pink and streaky?

The berries broke down, either from overmixing or from thawed frozen fruit. Add berries in the last 30-60 seconds on the lowest speed, and always add frozen berries straight from the freezer. A few pink streaks around each berry are normal and honestly pretty.

Does the orange juice hurt the yeast?

It slows things a little, which is why the bulk rise runs closer to 2 hours than 90 minutes. That's built into the schedule. Don't add extra yeast to compensate, you'd trade flavor for speed and win neither.

How does the sourdough timeline actually work for a weekend?

Build the levain Friday at 9 PM. Saturday: mix at 8 AM, bulk until about 1 PM, shape, then either proof warm and bake by 4:30 PM, or refrigerate the shaped loaf and bake Sunday at 8 AM straight from the fridge. The cold-retard route is the more forgiving of the two.

Can I use all-purpose flour?

Yes, with a slightly softer crumb. Hold back 15g of the milk and add it only if the dough feels dry, since all-purpose absorbs less.

How do I know it's actually done?

Temperature, not color. The crust looks done 10 minutes before the center is, thanks to the honey and juice. Pull it at 190°F (88°C) in the center. Under that, the berry pockets stay gummy.
